references.text: The context of who went up the mountain and saw God—Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders.
A parallel description that they saw the God of Israel, with a description of what was seen under his feet.
God says that no one can see his face and live, which stands in tension with the fact that the elders saw God and yet lived.
Jacob saw God face to face at Peniel and was still spared, a parallel to how Israel's leaders saw God and survived.
Manoah feared he would die because he had seen God, showing that seeing God was normally considered fatal.
Isaiah sees the Lord and fears for his life, a parallel to the theophany experience in Exodus 24.
Ezekiel sees the glory of the Lord, another theophany where the prophet survives the vision of God.
No one has ever seen God, but the Son has made him known—a theological reflection on how humans can see God.
God dwells in unapproachable light, and no one has seen or can see him—a theological statement about God's inaccessibility.
Blessed are those invited to the Lamb's wedding feast—an eschatological meal in God's presence, parallel to the meal at Sinai.
A parallel in the meal motif ('ate and drank') that marks a gracious conclusion to a conflict or holy meeting.
Contrastive parallel: A meal as a sign of a wrongful decision (Joshua) versus a meal as a sign of gracious reconciliation (Exodus).
